title: When the problem is really about ranking outcomes
reader_situation: You are looking at a story where nobody has made a strategic move yet. The hard part is simpler and earlier: one person has several possible outcomes, and you need to say which outcomes they would rather have.
diagnostic_question: Can I describe what this person wants before I describe how anyone reacts to anyone else?
first_principles_test: Start by separating desire from strategy. If changing another player's move is not the main issue yet, the right first move is to build a scale of better and worse outcomes. Preferences give the ordering; utility turns that ordering into numbers only when numbers help compare or calculate.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical object is an ordering or payoff map. In plain language, it is a disciplined way to say this outcome is preferred to that one, and sometimes by how much for the calculation at hand.
false_friend: Do not treat a payoff number as a physical measurement like height or weight. In many game theory uses, the number is a bookkeeping device for choices, not a direct measure of happiness.
where_to_go_next: Once the player's wants are clear, move to strategic-form or extensive-form representation if another player's choice changes what this person should do.

title: When the problem is really about drawing the situation correctly
reader_situation: You are given a messy interaction and feel tempted to solve it immediately. But the real bottleneck is that the order of moves, available actions, and information are not yet clear.
diagnostic_question: Would the answer change if I wrote the same story as a table instead of a tree?
first_principles_test: Ask what each player knows when they choose. If everyone chooses without seeing the others' current move, a table may be enough. If choices unfold over time, or later players observe earlier moves, the tree matters because timing can create or destroy credible threats.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical object is a representation of players, actions, timing, information, and payoffs. The math matters because different representations preserve different facts about the same story.
false_friend: Do not solve a game before checking whether the representation erased timing or information. A table can hide a threat that a tree exposes as not credible.
where_to_go_next: After the representation is honest, ask whether some actions can be eliminated or whether the prediction must survive mutual best responses.

title: When the problem is really about ruling out unreasonable moves
reader_situation: The game has too many possible choices, and some of them look foolish no matter what the other side does. The useful work is not predicting the final outcome yet; it is shrinking the possibility space.
diagnostic_question: Is there an action that is worse than another available action under every relevant comparison?
first_principles_test: Look for a move that can be beaten without needing a precise prediction of the opponent. Dominance and iterated deletion are pruning tools: they remove choices that cannot be justified by any sensible belief about the other player's behavior.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical lever is an inequality across payoffs. If one action always gives less than another against the same outside behavior, the weaker action can be deleted from serious consideration.
false_friend: Do not confuse unlikely with dominated. A move is not dominated merely because it sounds bad; it must lose under the comparison the model is actually making.
where_to_go_next: If pruning leaves several live possibilities, move to Nash equilibrium or mixed strategies to ask which choices can be mutually consistent.

title: When the problem is really about mutual consistency
reader_situation: Each player's best move depends on what the other players do. A recommendation that sounds good for one person may collapse once the others are allowed to respond.
diagnostic_question: If everyone heard the proposed prediction, would anyone want to change their own move?
first_principles_test: Hold the other players' choices fixed and ask whether each player is doing the best they can from their own point of view. Equilibrium is not moral approval and not group happiness; it is a no-one-wants-to-unilaterally-move test.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical object is a fixed point of best responses. In everyday terms, the prediction points back to itself: each part of the prediction gives the other parts a reason to stay in place.
false_friend: Do not read equilibrium as good, fair, efficient, or inevitable. It can be bad for everyone, and the course uses it because it is a disciplined prediction test, not because it is a welfare judgment.
where_to_go_next: If the game unfolds over time, test the equilibrium again inside every later subgame. If information is hidden, move to beliefs and Bayesian consistency.

title: When the problem is really about time and credibility
reader_situation: A player promises, threatens, delays, bargains, or plans to act later. The central question is whether a future action would still make sense when that future moment arrives.
diagnostic_question: Would the player still want to carry out the announced plan after reaching the point where the plan is supposed to happen?
first_principles_test: Reason from the end backward. A future threat only matters if it is optimal when the future decision point is actually reached. Backward induction and subgame perfection make the model check promises at the moment they must be honored.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical lever is recursion over time: solve the later choice, then use that answer when solving the earlier choice. The later self constrains what the earlier self can credibly claim.
false_friend: Do not accept a threat just because it changes today's incentives. If carrying it out tomorrow would hurt the threatener, the model treats it as empty unless another mechanism repairs credibility.
where_to_go_next: If the same players meet again and again, ask whether the future can discipline present behavior through repeated-game incentives.

title: When the problem is really about the future disciplining the present
reader_situation: The same players interact repeatedly, so today's selfish move may change tomorrow's treatment. The current action is also a signal about how the relationship will continue.
diagnostic_question: Is a short-run temptation being restrained by the value of future cooperation?
first_principles_test: Compare the one-time gain from deviating with the future loss from being punished or losing cooperation. Repetition matters when future consequences are large enough to change what is rational today.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical lever is discounting: future payoffs are counted, but usually with less weight than immediate payoffs. Cooperation can survive only when the discounted future is strong enough to outweigh the immediate temptation.
false_friend: Do not assume repetition automatically creates cooperation. If the end is known and close, or players care little about the future, the repeated game can unravel back toward one-shot behavior.
where_to_go_next: If players differ in hidden ways or observe different information, add beliefs and ask what each player can infer from what they see.

title: When the problem is really about hidden information
reader_situation: One side knows something the other side does not: a cost, value, quality, patience level, or outside option. The visible action is partly a choice and partly evidence about the hidden fact.
diagnostic_question: Am I trying to predict behavior when players disagree about what kind of person or situation they are facing?
first_principles_test: List the possible hidden types and ask what each type would do. Then ask how observers should update their beliefs after seeing an action. Hidden information turns strategy into a joint problem of choosing and interpreting.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical object is a belief over possible types, combined with payoffs conditional on those types. Bayes' rule enters when observed behavior changes which hidden type seems more likely.
false_friend: Do not treat a belief as a guess with no discipline. In Bayesian games and signaling settings, beliefs must be tied to the possible types, observed actions, and equilibrium logic.
where_to_go_next: If the informed player sends a message or takes an observable costly action, move to signaling or cheap talk and ask what communication can credibly reveal.

title: When the problem is really about rules shaping incentives
reader_situation: The main object is not a player choosing inside fixed rules, but the rules themselves: an auction format, market institution, ad slot system, contract, or communication protocol.
diagnostic_question: Would changing the rules change what people reveal, bid, produce, or hide?
first_principles_test: Treat rules as machines for translating private motives into observable behavior. A good mechanism makes the desired behavior individually sensible; a bad one rewards hiding, shading, collusion, or misleading signals.
mathematical_handle: The mathematical lever is incentive compatibility: the rule should make the intended action line up with each participant's own payoff calculation. Auctions, screening, and ad markets are different settings where that alignment is the design problem.
false_friend: Do not judge a rule only by the outcome it asks for. The question is whether self-interested participants have a reason to produce that outcome when the rule is actually used.
where_to_go_next: If the rule includes messages or public announcements, ask whether the information becomes shared knowledge or merely private interpretation.
